about.title: Roseville Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Roseville's economy runs on people who work with their hands, drive for a living, or spend long shifts on their feet — warehouse crews near I-80, retail and restaurant staff along Douglas Boulevard, delivery drivers threading Pleasant Grove Boulevard and Cirby Way, and construction teams across Placer County. When one of those workdays ends in an injury, the path forward is rarely one form. Workers' compensation covers most on-the-job injuries in California no matter who was at fault, and it is generally your only claim against your employer. But many Roseville injuries involve someone outside the company: a subcontractor on a shared job site, a property owner who let a hazard sit, a manufacturer whose equipment failed, or another motorist. Roseville logged 808 injury collisions in 2025, with 1,156 people hurt, and workers driving for their jobs are part of that count. Those third-party situations can open a separate injury claim alongside your comp benefits. LawProactive connects you, at no cost, with an independent attorney who can sort out which applies to you.

items.title: We know where comp stops and a claim begins

items.title: Deadlines get watched from day one

items.question: I was hit on I-80 while driving a company vehicle in Roseville. Is that a workers' comp case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It can be both. Because you were working, workers' compensation should cover your medical care and part of your lost wages regardless of who caused the crash. If another driver was negligent, you may also have a separate third-party injury claim against that driver, which can cover losses comp does not. An attorney can coordinate the two so one does not undercut the other.

items.question: Can my Roseville employer fire me for reporting an injury or filing a claim?
items.answer: No. Retaliating against a worker for reporting an injury or pursuing workers' compensation is illegal in California. Report the injury to your employer within 30 days to protect your benefits, and keep a copy of what you submitted. If you are demoted, cut from the schedule, or let go afterward, tell the attorney you are connected with right away.

items.question: A subcontractor's crew left a hazard on our Placer County job site and I got hurt. Who do I go after?
items.answer: Your own employer is generally shielded by workers' comp, but a separate company on the same site is not. If the subcontractor's negligence caused your injury, you may be able to bring a third-party claim against that business in addition to collecting comp benefits. These claims carry a two-year deadline, so it helps to have someone evaluate the facts early.
